explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jesus says, “…they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat.” They've been with Him three days and have nothing to eat, and He doesn't brush it off. He says right out, “I have compassion for this crowd…” That's the heart of this whole story.

Forty is a big Bible number, friend, so I see why it jumped out. But in this scene Jesus says the crowd has been with Him three days. Nobody here is counting forty. The crowd being with Him three days and having nothing to eat is plenty for Him to say He has compassion.

Ten days with no food would be a whole different situation, baker. Jesus says, “…they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat.” Three is the number. And it's already enough for Him to say, “I have compassion for this crowd…”

explanations.answer: They will faint along the way
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “If I send them home hungry, they will faint along the way.” He adds, “For some of them have come a great distance.” I think He's looking down the road, and that's what compassion looks like: already thinking about the trip home.

explanations.answer: They will get lost in the dark
explanations.explanation: Nothing about darkness here, friend. Jesus doesn't bring up the dark or getting lost. What He says is that if He sends them home hungry, “…they will faint along the way.” His worry is empty stomachs on a long walk.

Jesus doesn't say a word about grumbling, baker. His concern is their bodies, not their attitude. He says, “If I send them home hungry, they will faint along the way.” That's compassion talking, not a complaint department.

True, friend. Jesus says, “For some of them have come a great distance.” So this isn't just a neighborhood crowd. Some of these folks traveled far, and they're now far from a meal too. That makes sending them home hungry an even harder walk.

Not quite, baker. Jesus says it Himself: “For some of them have come a great distance.” So the text says some of the crowd traveled far. That's part of why He says they would faint along the way if sent home hungry.

explanations.answer: Where could anyone find enough bread to feed them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The disciples ask, “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” They're looking around at empty land and a huge crowd. I think I'd be asking the same thing. Good thing Jesus has a plan.

explanations.answer: Why not send them to the nearby villages
explanations.explanation: The disciples never suggest villages, friend. Their question is about bread: “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” They're stuck on how to feed everybody right where they are.

explanations.answer: How will we get them all home safely
explanations.explanation: Getting them home was Jesus' worry, baker. He's the one who says they'd faint along the way. The disciples ask something else: “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” Their eyes are on the missing bread.
Seven it is, baker. Jesus asks, “How many loaves do you have?” and they reply, “Seven.” Seven loaves for a crowd that big. I've stretched a batch before, but never THAT far, friend.

Close, but no, friend. When Jesus asks how many loaves they have, the disciples reply, “Seven.” Nine would be two extra loaves, and those two aren't in this story. Seven is what they've got, and it's what Jesus uses.

Four does show up in this passage, baker, but it's in the number of men: about four thousand were present (Mark 8:9). The loaves are a different count. The disciples answer Jesus' question with “Seven.”

Right, baker. The text says Jesus “…instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground.” Nothing is handed out yet. First the whole crowd settles in, and then He takes the loaves. I think a seated crowd means everybody's getting fed, friend.

Groups of fifty belong to a different feeding. In Luke 9:14, Jesus tells His disciples to have the people sit down in groups of about fifty each. Here in Mark 8, the text says He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. No group sizes this time, friend.

No shore in this scene, baker. Before the bread comes out, Jesus “…instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground.” That's the instruction. The boat doesn't come into it until after everyone has eaten.

Yes, baker. The text says Jesus “…took the seven loaves, gave thanks and broke them…” He gives thanks first, with seven loaves in His hands in front of a huge crowd. Then comes the breaking. That's worth remembering the next time you face a table that looks too small.
Jesus does give an order in this scene, friend, but it goes to the crowd: sit down. With the loaves, the text says He “…gave thanks and broke them…” Thanks is the word that fits here.
No warning with the loaves, baker. The text says Jesus “…took the seven loaves, gave thanks and broke them…” A warning does come later in this passage, in the boat. At the loaves, it's thanks.

True, baker. Jesus broke the loaves and gave them to His disciples “…to set before the people.” Then the text says they “…distributed them to the crowd.” So the disciples carried the bread out to the crowd. They're in the middle of it, handing out food that came from seven loaves.
Not false, friend. The text says Jesus gave the bread to His disciples “…to set before the people.” And they distributed it to the crowd. The disciples did the serving, and Jesus did the giving.
Not quite, baker. The text says, “The people ate and were satisfied…” That covers the whole crowd, not just some of it. Seven loaves and a few small fish, and nobody was left out.
False is right, friend. “The people ate and were satisfied…” Everybody, not just the folks up front. Seven loaves and a few small fish, and that crowd walked away full.

True, baker. They started with seven loaves, and the disciples “…picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.” Seven in, seven baskets out, after a whole crowd was satisfied. I'd call that a pretty good return, friend.

Check the numbers again, baker. The disciples started with seven loaves (Mark 8:5). After everyone ate, they “…picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.” Seven and seven, and a crowd fed in between.
That's it, baker. The text says Jesus “…immediately got into the boat with His disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.” Right after the crowd leaves, He's off. You nailed it.

Bethsaida is a real place, friend, but it's not the stop here. After He dismissed the crowd, Jesus got into the boat with His disciples and went to “…the district of Dalmanutha.” That's where the boat lands in this story.

Capernaum doesn't come up in this passage, baker. After sending the crowd off, Jesus “…immediately got into the boat with His disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.” Dalmanutha is the name to remember.
That's it, baker. The Pharisees were “…testing Him by demanding from Him a sign from heaven.” The text says they came and began to argue with Jesus. A sign is what they demanded.
Nothing about family lines here, friend. The text says the Pharisees came and began to argue with Jesus, “…testing Him by demanding from Him a sign from heaven.” That's their demand.
They weren't asking for a ruling, baker. The Pharisees argued with Jesus, “…testing Him by demanding from Him a sign from heaven.” A sign is what they wanted, and they wanted it from heaven.

That's not what Jesus says, friend. His words: “Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.” He doesn't promise it. He says it won't be given. He also sighs deeply in His spirit before He says it.

False, and Jesus is clear about it. He says, “Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.” No promise, no maybe later. He sighed deeply in His spirit first, baker, so I think this one weighed on Him.
One loaf, baker. The text says the disciples “…had forgotten to take bread, except for one loaf they had with them in the boat.” One loaf for a boatful of disciples. That's a tight lunch, friend.
The count is lower than that, baker. The text says they forgot bread “…except for one loaf…” Just one. Two loaves would have been twice what they had, friend.
Six would be a pretty good stash, friend, but it's not what the text says. The disciples forgot bread, “…except for one loaf they had with them in the boat.” One loaf is all they had.

Yes, baker. Jesus cautions them, “Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.” Herod was ruler of Galilee (Luke 3:1), and Jesus names him right alongside the Pharisees. Leaven is what makes dough rise, and that's the word Jesus picks.
No swords in this warning, friend. Jesus says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.” The word is leaven. The text doesn't mention a single weapon.
Taxes aren't mentioned here, baker. Jesus says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.” Leaven is the word, and it's a baker's word, so listen up.

True, friend. The text says Jesus was “Aware of their conversation…” The disciples were talking with one another about having no bread, and He knew it. Then He asks them, “Why are you debating about having no bread?”

Not false, baker. The text says Jesus was “Aware of their conversation…” They were discussing having no bread, and He knew what they were talking about. That's why He asks them, “Why are you debating about having no bread?”

That's the point, baker. Jesus asks, “Do you still not see or understand?” and goes on, “‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’…” In this very passage, seven loaves fed the crowd, and now the disciples are debating about having no bread.

explanations.answer: They are too tired to listen
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about tiredness, friend. He asks, “Do you still not see or understand?” His question is about understanding, not energy. Seeing and hearing are the point here.

explanations.answer: They should stay away from crowds
explanations.explanation: Crowds aren't the issue, baker. Jesus had just fed one, with compassion. His question to the disciples is, “Do you still not see or understand?” That's what He's getting at.

Twelve, baker. Jesus asks, “When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” and they answer, “Twelve.” Five loaves went out, and twelve baskets came back. The disciples knew the number, and then Jesus asks, “Do you still not understand?”

Eight isn't the number, friend. When Jesus asks about the five loaves and the five thousand, the disciples answer, “Twelve.” Twelve baskets of broken pieces, and Mark 6:43 says those baskets held bread and fish.
That's too many baskets, baker. The disciples tell Jesus, “Twelve.” That's already a lot of leftovers from five loaves. No need to pad it.

That's not how it goes, friend. After the disciples answer, Jesus asks them, “Do you still not understand?” The passage ends on His question, with no announcement that they finally understand. He leaves them with something to think about.
False, baker. After they answer “Twelve” and “Seven,” Jesus asks, “Do you still not understand?” That's where the passage ends. Jesus doesn't say they finally get it. He ends on the question.
